title: Nsiho
author: Ghanaian tradition
desc: Made from dehulled maize so it comes out white — steeped forty-eight hours to pH 3.58, then a short twelve-hour dough ferment to pH 3.50.
longDesc: Nsiho is white kenkey, and the whiteness comes from dehulling the maize before anything else. It is the best-quantified fermentation in the Ghanaian literature because two University of Ghana theses measured it stage by stage. Traditional steeping runs forty-eight hours, during which pH falls from 5.99 to 3.58 and titratable acidity climbs from 0.03 to 0.30 per cent. The dough then ferments only twelve hours, pH falling from 5.94 to 3.50. One thesis optimised the process at thirty to forty-five hours of steeping at thirty to thirty-five degrees followed by twelve hours of dough fermentation.
ingredients: Water, for steeping and for the dough
// Quantities are not published in any named source. See the note.
steps: Dehull the white maize — this is what makes nsiho white rather than cream.
Steep the dehulled grain in water 48 hours at ambient temperature, or 30 to 45 hours at 30 to 35 degrees for the optimised process.
// STEEPING ENDPOINT: pH falls from about 5.99 to about 3.58, with titratable acidity rising from about 0.03 to 0.30 per cent.
Mill the steeped grain to a dough.
// DOUGH ENDPOINT: pH falls from about 5.94 to about 3.50, with titratable acidity rising from about 0.27 to 0.36 per cent.
Cook part of the dough into a thick paste and fold the raw remainder back in.
Shape, wrap, and steam or boil until cooked through.
// The finished product should be whitish, with a fruity odour and a smooth, non-sticky texture, and only mildly sour.
chefTips: Dehulling is the whole point. Leave the hulls on and you have ordinary kenkey; take them off and you get the pale colour and the much milder flavour nsiho is wanted for.
Two separate ferments with very different lengths: forty-eight hours for the steep, only twelve for the dough. Most of the souring happens before the grain is even milled.
The target is mildly sour, not strongly so. Consumers in the published study liked a whitish colour, a fruity odour, and a smooth non-sticky texture with minimal sourness.
A fruity odour rather than a sharply sour one is the sensory marker — this is the gentlest of the kenkey family.
Thirty to forty-five hours at thirty to thirty-five degrees is the optimised steep. A warm spot shortens it; a cool kitchen lengthens it.
Vendor samples measured pH 4.07 to 4.54 in the finished product, which is higher — less sour — than ordinary kenkey's 3.7.
Published as a process. No named source gives household quantities and none have been invented.
commonMistakes: Giving the dough the same long ferment as the steep.
Fermenting to the sourness of ordinary kenkey.
Letting it go sticky, which the published consumer work identifies as a fault.
Expecting home measurements, which do not exist in print.
sources: PUBLISHED AS A DOCUMENTED PROCESS, NOT A HOUSEHOLD RECIPE. NO NAMED SOURCE PUBLISHES QUANTITIES; none have been invented and the ingredient list says so.
PRIMARY SOURCE: Annan T., 'Development of Starter Culture for the Fermentation of Dehulled Maize into Nsiho (White Kenkey)', thesis, University of Ghana, 2013. TWO-PASS across two links.
STEEPING, 48 hours, verbatim: 'Mean pH values decreased from 5.99-3.58 units'. Titratable acidity 'increased from 0.03-0.30 %'.
DOUGH FERMENTATION, 12 hours, verbatim: 'pH values decreased from 5.94-3.50 units'. Titratable acidity 'increased from 0.27-0.36 %'.

Also from that thesis: traditional nsiho steeping is 48 h and dough fermentation up to 24 h; the starter culture it developed cut steeping to 24 h. Organisms identified: L. fermentum 47.1%, L. brevis 25%, L. plantarum 14.42%, Pediococcus pentosaceus 8.65%, P. acidilactici 4.8%; yeasts S. cerevisiae 47.6%, C. krusei 29.1%, Debaryomyces 15%, Trichosporon 8.3%.

THE OPTIMISED PROCESS and the consumer sensory targets: Oduro-Yeboah C., 'Process Optimization and Product Characteristics of White Kenkey (Nsiho)', PhD thesis, University of Ghana, 2015. TWO-PASS: the optimal process is '30-45 h at 30-35ºC temperature followed by 12 h dough fermentation'. SINGLE-PASS: vendor samples had pH 4.07-4.54, titratable acidity '0.42-0.60% lactic acid', moisture 70-77%, and consumers liked a 'whitish colour, fruity odour, smooth and non-sticky texture' with minimal sourness.
A GAP IN THAT SOURCE: the full thesis PDF returned HTTP 500, so its stage-by-stage pH tables were not read. The figures above come from its abstract and repository record.

WHY THIS IS THE BEST-QUANTIFIED FERMENTATION IN THE GHANAIAN RECORD: it has two separately measured stages with start and end pH, titratable acidity for both, a temperature, an optimised duration, a named organism profile, AND consumer sensory targets. Nothing else in this collection — Ghanaian or Nigerian — is documented to that standard.
NOTE THE FINISHED pH: vendor samples at 4.07-4.54 are markedly less acidic than ordinary kenkey's roughly 3.7 (see GHA037 and GHA038), which matches the consumer preference for minimal sourness.
RELATED but not this product: a nsiho milling paper on ResearchGate was unreachable (HTTP 429).
storage: Shorter-keeping than ordinary kenkey because it is less acidic. 2 to 3 days refrigerated.
healthBenefits: Dehulling removes some fibre but also most of the phytate, improving mineral absorption.
Milder acidity makes it easier on sensitive stomachs than ordinary kenkey.
culturalNote: White kenkey is the gentler member of the family — paler, fruitier, barely sour — and it is often what gets given to children or to someone who finds ordinary kenkey too sharp. It is also, by a wide margin, the best-documented fermented food in Ghana, thanks to two University of Ghana theses that measured every stage.
